title: Knowledge Check 8 - Lessons 36-42
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 36-42 - Data Migration | Data Modeling/Database Design. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: A migration from three source systems into Accounts produces duplicates in Salesforce. What was most likely missing?
options: A bigger batch size
Cross-source identity resolution applied before loading
More validation rules
A page layout per source
questions.explanation: Without identity resolution across sources, the same customer is loaded three times; batch size, validation rules, and layouts do not prevent cross-source duplicates.

questions.question: Which TWO practices ensure every source row is accounted for after migration?
options: A rejects/error file with reasons for invalid rows
Dropping rows that fail validation
Reconciliation of loaded/merged/rejected counts against the source extract
Ignoring lookup resolution failures
questions.explanation: An error file with reasons (A) and count reconciliation (C) account for every row; dropping silently (B) or ignoring lookup failures (D) hides data loss.

questions.question: Source picklist values include codes that do not exist in the target picklist. What is the correct approach?
options: Load them anyway
Map each source value to a valid target value or a default/Unknown value before loading
Remove the picklist from the target
Convert the field to text
questions.explanation: Unmapped values cause load failures, so map to valid target values or a documented default; the other options create invalid data or degrade the model.

questions.question: A 12-million-row load fails with 'unable to obtain row lock' when Contacts and their parent Accounts load concurrently. Which change most directly fixes this?
options: Increase the batch size
Load parents first and use serial mode (or group by parent) to avoid lock contention
Switch to the synchronous SOAP API
Disable duplicate rules
questions.explanation: Parent lock contention is solved by ordering/grouping by parent and using serial mode; bigger batches (A) worsen it, synchronous APIs (C) are slower, and duplicate rules (D) are unrelated.

questions.question: Which TWO are appropriate performance choices for an LDV migration?
options: Using Bulk API with tuned batch sizes and parent-before-child ordering
Loading all objects in maximum parallel mode regardless of parents
Deferring sharing calculation and scheduling the load off-peak
Using the synchronous REST API for millions of records
questions.explanation: Bulk API with tuned batches/ordering (A) and deferred sharing + off-peak scheduling (C) are sound; uncontrolled parallelism (B) and synchronous APIs (D) are anti-patterns.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off between Bulk API serial and parallel modes?
options: Serial is faster but risks lock contention; parallel is slower and safer
Parallel is faster but risks record-lock contention; serial avoids contention at the cost of speed
They are identical in behavior
Serial cannot load related objects
questions.explanation: Parallel mode is faster but can cause lock contention on shared parents; serial mode processes sequentially to avoid contention but runs slower.

questions.question: A business-critical migration cannot tolerate a long downtime but has 40 million records. Which approach best minimizes the freeze window?
options: A single big-bang load on cutover weekend
Initial full load plus continuous delta sync until a short final cutover
Manual weekend re-entry
Loading only current-year data
questions.explanation: Initial full load + delta sync shrinks the freeze to the final delta; big-bang (A) needs a long freeze, and the others do not meet the requirement.

questions.question: Which TWO are elements of a sound cutover plan?
options: A rehearsed final delta sync with measured timing
Immediate decommission of the legacy system at cutover
Go/no-go checks and a defined rollback window
No user communication until after cutover
questions.explanation: A rehearsed/timed delta (A) and go/no-go + rollback window (C) are essential; immediate decommission (B) removes rollback and silence (D) creates confusion.

questions.question: Why is incremental migration often chosen for large, business-critical programs?
options: It eliminates the need for a delta sync
It reduces risk and downtime by moving data in waves while testing between them
It avoids all data-quality work
It requires no rollback plan
questions.explanation: Waves reduce risk and allow learning, though they require parallel-run sync (A false); quality work (C) and rollback planning (D) are still required.

questions.question: A team needs a recurring nightly feed of changed records to a warehouse. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Weekly Data Export files
Bulk API query jobs extracting incrementally by SystemModstamp
Report exports
List view exports
questions.explanation: Recurring incremental extraction for a warehouse uses Bulk API/ETL with last-modified filters; Data Export (A) is scheduled backup and reports/list views (C, D) are limited and not for feeds.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about Salesforce exports are TRUE?
options: Report exports are limited by row limits and not suited to LDV
Exports include all data regardless of the running user's access
Scheduled Data Export is a coarse backup, not a full point-in-time restore
Exports can be non-selective without performance impact
questions.explanation: Report exports have row limits (A) and Data Export is coarse backup only (C); exports are filtered by the user's access (B false) and LDV exports must be selective (D false).

questions.question: Why must large exports filter on indexed fields?
options: Because exports cannot use SOQL
Because non-selective queries time out at LDV, so indexed filters keep extraction performant
Because reports require it
Because encryption requires it
questions.explanation: LDV exports must be selective to avoid timeouts; exports do use SOQL (A false) and the other reasons are unrelated.

questions.question: A warehouse feed pulls changed records by SystemModstamp but never reflects deletions. What is the fix?
options: Increase the batch size
Use Change Data Capture delete events or run a periodic id-set reconciliation to detect deletes
Switch to report exports
Enable duplicate rules
questions.explanation: Last-modified extracts miss deletes; CDC delete events or reconciliation detects them. Batch size, report exports, and duplicate rules do not address deletions.

questions.question: Which TWO are required before deleting data from Salesforce after an archival export?
options: Verify the export is complete and restorable/queryable
Delete immediately to free storage
Reconcile exported counts against Salesforce
Encrypt the source records in place
questions.explanation: Completeness/restorability verification (A) and count reconciliation (C) must precede deletion; deleting first (B) risks data loss and in-place encryption (D) is unrelated.

questions.question: Why chunk a large-volume export by date or id range?
options: To reduce data quality
To bound job size, avoid timeouts, and stay within API limits
Because Bulk API forbids large queries
To avoid needing an index
questions.explanation: Chunking keeps jobs small, avoids timeouts, and respects limits; it does not reduce quality (A) and indexing is still required (D).

questions.question: A bulk integration assigns all 30 million loaded records to a single integration user; sharing recalculation is very slow. What is the fix?
options: Add more sharing rules
Distribute ownership across multiple integration users/queues
Remove the role hierarchy
Enable Platform Encryption
questions.explanation: Extreme ownership skew is fixed by distributing owners; more rules (A) worsen recalculation, and removing the hierarchy/encryption do not address skew.

questions.question: Which TWO are advanced mitigations for extreme lookup/roll-up skew?
options: Replace live roll-ups on the skewed MD relationship with a scheduled aggregation to a denormalized field
Add another roll-up summary to the hot parent
Shard the relationship by introducing intermediate parents
Keep loading children in maximum parallel mode
questions.explanation: Replacing live roll-ups with scheduled aggregation (A) and sharding via intermediate parents (C) relieve the hot parent; more roll-ups (B) and max parallelism (D) worsen contention.

questions.question: Why is mass-reparenting high-volume children dangerous under skew?
options: It changes the record's data type
It fans out locking and cascade operations across millions of children, causing timeouts and lock errors
It disables validation rules
It removes external IDs
questions.explanation: Reparenting under skew spreads lock/cascade load across millions of records, causing timeouts; it does not change data types, disable validation, or remove external IDs.

questions.question: A cutover's final delta sync is taking far longer than planned because change volume since the last sync was underestimated. What was missing?
options: A larger batch size
A rehearsed, timed cutover runbook that measured the final delta sync realistically
More duplicate rules
A Big Object archive
questions.explanation: Only a rehearsed, timed runbook reveals realistic delta duration; batch size, duplicate rules, and archives do not address cutover timing.

questions.question: Which TWO are essential elements of a migration rollback plan?
options: Defined rollback triggers and authorized decision-makers
Immediate decommission of the legacy system at cutover
Keeping the legacy system available read-only for a viability window
Skipping post-go-live validation
questions.explanation: Rollback needs triggers/authority (A) and a read-only legacy window (C); immediate decommission (B) removes the rollback path and skipping validation (D) hides issues.

questions.question: Which activity belongs to post-go-live validation rather than pre-cutover?
options: Profiling the source data
Dry-run load in a full sandbox
Reconciling counts/aggregates and validating integrations and access after go-live
Writing the mapping document
questions.explanation: Post-go-live validation reconciles counts, validates integrations, and checks access on the live system; profiling/ dry-run / mapping are pre-migration activities.
